articles.title: New Zealand Signed a Trade Deal With India. Then It Quietly Started Writing Immigration Rules That Apply to Indians — and Only Indians.
articles.excerpt: Even NZ's own Foreign Minister calls the proposed restrictions discriminatory. Days before Modi's first-ever visit, the country's coalition government is tearing itself apart over who gets to come in.
articles.image_caption: New Zealand's Parliament House in Wellington, where the ruling coalition is divided over immigration rules that single out Indian nationals under the newly signed free trade agreement.
articles.nri_angle: New Zealand's proposed immigration restrictions specifically target Indian nationals, affecting NRI workers, students, and the 250,000-strong Indian diaspora community — with racist rhetoric and anti-Indian protests compounding the policy threat
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The USISPF Summit Honoured Three Business Titans. Sunil Mittal Used His Speech to Talk About Five Million Indians Instead.
articles.excerpt: At the IX USISPF Leadership Summit in Washington, Bharti's chairman and India's ambassador to the US laid out a vision in which the diaspora is not a footnote to the India-US partnership but the load-bearing wall.
articles.image_caption: Sunil Bharti Mittal, founder and chairman of Bharti Enterprises
articles.nri_angle: Mittal explicitly framed the 5-million-strong Indian American community as the strategic bridge between India and the US — in trade, defence, and high technology. Ambassador Kwatra's $30 trillion roadmap positions the diaspora as investors, knowledge partners, and connectors in India's climb to developed-nation status by 2047.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Sitharaman Took India's Chequebook to France. She Is Ending the Trip by Meeting the Diaspora.
articles.excerpt: India's finance minister co-chaired an economic dialogue in Aix-en-Provence, courted BNP Paribas and a cargo airship startup, and will wrap up her four-day visit with a community event for Indians in France — the quiet end of a loud trip.
articles.image_caption: Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman during a European engagement in 2025
articles.nri_angle: Sitharaman's France visit concludes with a diaspora community interaction, connecting India's economic diplomacy directly to the 30,000-strong Indian community in France. India-France trade has doubled in a decade to €13.59 billion, and the India-EU FTA signed in January 2026 opens new pathways for NRIs across Europe.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Indian Immigrants Have Built 96 Billion-Dollar Startups in America. No Other Country Comes Close.
articles.excerpt: A new NFAP study finds India is the largest source of immigrant unicorn founders in the US, with 96 companies collectively worth more than Germany's stock market.
articles.image_caption: Jyoti Bansal, Indian-born founder of AppDynamics and Harness, at TechCrunch Disrupt 2024 — one of 96 Indian immigrant-founded US unicorn startups identified in the NFAP study (Photo: TechCrunch/Katelyn Tucker, CC BY 2.0)
articles.nri_angle: Indian-born entrepreneurs account for 96 of America's 775 unicorns — the most of any country. Most arrived as IIT graduates on student visas, building the exact pipeline now threatened by tightening H-1B and student visa policies.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Carnegie Names Four Indian Americans to Its 'Great Immigrants' List — on the Eve of America's 250th Birthday
articles.excerpt: Nikesh Arora, Mahzarin Banaji, Sanjiv Chopra, and Reshma Kewalramani join a class of 25 naturalized citizens honoured by the Carnegie Corporation for the Fourth of July.
articles.image_caption: Nikesh Arora, chairman and CEO of Palo Alto Networks, one of four Indian Americans named to Carnegie's 2026 Great Immigrants list
articles.nri_angle: Four Indian-born leaders — spanning cybersecurity, social psychology, medicine, and biotech — are honoured as 'Great Americans' at a moment when immigration restrictions are tightening. The recognition underscores the diaspora's institutional reach across American life.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: New US Bill Would End OPT, Kill H-1B Green Card Pathway in Sweeping Overhaul
articles.excerpt: Rep. Chip Roy’s American White-Collar Worker Jobs Act targets every stage of the Indian professional immigration pipeline, from student work permits to permanent residency
articles.image_caption: The US Capitol, where Rep. Chip Roy introduced the American White-Collar Worker Jobs Act of 2026 targeting the H-1B visa program.
articles.nri_angle: Indians hold 72% of H-1B visas and rely on OPT and the H-1B-to-green-card pipeline that this bill would dismantle — a direct threat to the immigration pathway used by hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Two Thousand Indian-Origin Doctors Just Took Over Tampa's Waterfront. The Timing Was Not an Accident.
articles.excerpt: AAPI's 44th annual convention opens on America's 250th birthday weekend, blending scientific sessions with a red-carpet civic reception from the City of Tampa.
articles.image_caption: Healthcare professionals in a hospital setting — Indian-origin physicians form one of the largest ethnic groups in American medicine
articles.nri_angle: Indian-origin physicians form one of the largest ethnic groups in American medicine. AAPI's convention, timed to America's 250th, is both a professional assembly and a statement of belonging.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Nine Hundred Young Jains Just Sold Out a Convention in New Jersey. Their Theme: 'The Art of the In-Between.'
articles.excerpt: The 17th biennial Young Jains of America convention opens this week with 915 attendees across three age cohorts — every spot taken, every waitlist full.
articles.image_caption: Jain community celebrations at a temple in New York City
articles.nri_angle: Young Jain Americans navigate between an ancient faith built on non-violence and non-attachment and a consumer culture that runs on the opposite. YJA's sold-out convention is the infrastructure they built for that in-between.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Just Killed the Physical OCI Booklet. Five Million Cardholders Can Finally Exhale.
articles.excerpt: The new e-OCI card lets overseas Indians complete the entire OCI lifecycle on a phone — no consular visits, no duplicate paperwork, no reissue anxiety.
articles.image_caption: Union Home Minister Amit Shah, who launched the e-OCI Card system in New Delhi
articles.nri_angle: Eliminates the single biggest bureaucratic pain point for 5M+ OCI holders worldwide — the mandatory physical booklet reissue that required consular visits, mailed documents, and weeks of waiting every time a passport was renewed.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Leicester's South Asian Arts Festival Turns Fifteen. The City Barely Notices — It Has Been Living This for Decades.
articles.excerpt: An Indian Summer returns to Leicester Cathedral, Jubilee Square, and Attenborough Arts Centre this week with five days of theatre, music, film, and dance.
articles.image_caption: Leicester's Belgrave Road area, known as the 'Golden Mile' — the cultural heart of one of Britain's most prominent South Asian communities
articles.nri_angle: Highlights how Leicester's concentrated South Asian diaspora sustains a 15-year-old contemporary arts festival — a model for diaspora cultural institutions that create shared physical space for identity beyond streaming and WhatsApp groups.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Supreme Court Just Ruled 6-3 That Children of H-1B Parents Born in America Are Citizens. No President Can Change That.
articles.excerpt: In a landmark ruling, the conservative-majority court struck down Trump's executive order targeting birthright citizenship — a decision that Indian American advocacy groups are calling 'a profound affirmation of who belongs in America.'
articles.image_caption: The United States Supreme Court in Washington, D.C.
articles.nri_angle: Indian families on H-1B and L-1 visas, who face the longest green card backlogs in the system, now have Supreme Court confirmation that their U.S.-born children's citizenship is constitutionally protected.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: America Turns 250. The Indian Diaspora Is Celebrating with Both Flags.
articles.excerpt: From a packed curtain raiser in Mineola to a tall ship in Baltimore Harbour, Indian Americans are weaving their story into the semiquincentennial — while already rehearsing for India's 80th.
articles.image_caption: The annual India Day Parade in New York City — Indian Americans celebrate their dual identity as America marks its 250th (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: The Indian-American community is uniquely positioned this summer, celebrating America's 250th birthday while preparing for India's 80th Independence Day — a dual-calendar life that defines the diaspora experience.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Three Bay Area Temples Hit in Three Weeks. The Diaspora Is Running Out of Cheeks to Turn.
articles.excerpt: Pro-Khalistan graffiti at a Swaminarayan mandir, a copycat attack in Hayward, and a burglary at a third temple have shaken Silicon Valley's Indian-American heartland — and renewed a question the community has never been able to put down.
articles.image_caption: A BAPS Swaminarayan Mandir in California, similar to the temples targeted in the Bay Area attacks
articles.nri_angle: The Bay Area temple attacks strike at the heart of the Indian-American community's sense of belonging — raising the question of whether success and visibility have made the diaspora a target rather than a shield.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Diaspora's Highest-Ranking AI Voice in Washington Just Walked Out of the White House
articles.excerpt: Sriram Krishnan's six-month run as Trump's senior AI policy adviser ends today. He's not done with Washington — he's just changing the address.
articles.image_caption: Sriram Krishnan, who served as senior White House AI policy adviser
articles.nri_angle: Krishnan's trajectory from Chennai to the West Wing represents a new frontier for Indian-American influence — policy, not just corporate leadership — and his departure raises the question of who fills the gap.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: He Sent ₹11 Lakh to His Parents. India's Tax Department Took Six Years to Believe It Was a Gift.
articles.excerpt: A US-based NRI's routine family transfer turned into a protracted legal battle. The case is a masterclass in what every diaspora family sending money home gets wrong.
articles.image_caption: The Income Tax Department of India — NRI remittances can trigger scrutiny if not properly documented (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Millions of NRIs send money to family in India every year with minimal documentation. This case shows exactly how that can go wrong — and what to do about it.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk
